transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-28 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Maya Chen (Redwood SE); Samir Patel (Redwood Solutions); Alex Ramos (Coppergate CTO); Priya Nair (Coppergate PM); Jamal Ortiz (Coppergate SRE); Hannah Lee (Coppergate Security)

Summary: quick walkthrough of JSON-mode and tool calling, demo of typed responses and runtime fallbacks, discussion about a 6-week pilot in VPC with audit requirements.

00:00 Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for making time, we called this short to run through JSON mode, show some guardrails and then talk pilot. alex, priya, jamal, hannah - thanks for joining.
00:18 Alex Ramos: Yeah, thanks. Quick context - we're building an LLM routing layer for shipping ETA and exception classification to ops teams. Need structured outputs, deterministic schema and strict data controls. Latency budget is tight, 80 p95 under 300ms if possible.
00:34 Jordan Lee: great, that's exactly the space JSON-mode is built for — typed responses and tool invocation so you can return a strict object that your downstream services can rely on. maya will kick off with a quick live demo.
00:48 Maya Chen: okay, so here's a quick demo deck link i've dropped in the chat, and i'll share my screen. i'm going to show a sample schema. people, you'll see we define a top-level object: status, eta_seconds, confidence_score, and actions[] which can invoke tools like "create_ticket" or "update_routing".
01:15 Maya Chen: (demo) i'm sending the same prompt to two runtime profiles: hosted low-cost and dedicated low-latency. watch the typed response enforcement — when the model returns off-schema we show structured fallback and a validation error that triggers a safe-tool-call to the sanbox checker.
01:38 Priya Nair: pause — can you show what happens if the model hallucinated an extra field name or used a string where a number is expected?
01:45 Maya Chen: yep, so in the console you see the validator kicks in, it can either coerce types, reject, or route the request to a deterministic runtime we call "strict-mode". we also have a fallback policy: if validate fails, call the sanbox validation tool (we call it "schema-checker") and then either return a supervised patch or call a human-in-the-loop.
02:12 Jamal Ortiz: how intrusive is that to our current flow? we have a microservice that only accepts a JSON with eta_seconds as integer and an enum status.
02:20 Maya Chen: minimal code changes — you receive the same object shape from the Redwood API. The big change is adding the schema to the model invocation or via the API header. client side you can configure auto-coerce or strict reject.
02:34 Hannah Lee: security — do you store requests? how long? we need audit logs and key management details.
02:42 Samir Patel: good question. we support configurable retention — default is 30 days in hosted, but for a VPC/private deployment you can disable retention and ship logs to your own SIEM. we integrate with KMS/HSM for key rotation, SSO via SAML, and RBAC for access. we also have per-token tracing in the console for cost/latency breakdowns.
03:10 Alex Ramos: you mentioned KV cache earlier in your doc, how does that affect freshness for ETAs?
03:17 Maya Chen: KV cache stores recent prefix states for auto-completion and speed. for ETA use case, you can scope cache by customer ID and TTL so stale predictions are invalidated. we recommended short TTLs like 30s for fast-moving routes. cache reduces per-token cost but you can disable it for strict freshness.
03:38 Priya Nair: demo time — can you show a tool-call where the model decides to open a ticket in our system?
03:45 Maya Chen: yes, so here the model returns an actions array with action: create_ticket and payload: {order_id, reason}. The runtime maps actions to your webhook or function endpoints. if the call fails we have an orchestration fallback chain: retry, route to alternate endpoint, or emit an alert and return a 503 with a graceful message.
04:12 Jordan Lee: we also provide typed-interfaces for these tool outputs, so your downstream workers can deserialize safely, and we log the chain for audits.
04:28 Jamal Ortiz: do you support on-prem? our security team is wary of anything hosted.
04:33 Samir Patel: yes — Redwood Private can run in your VPC or on-prem. the control plane can be customer-managed. we can provide an air-gapped package; that typically adds some lead time for deployment and ops handover. also Dedicated pools are an intermediary if you want isolation without full private.
04:56 Hannah Lee: what about SOC2 and ISO artifacts? we need certs and details on penetration testing and separation of duties.
05:02 Jordan Lee: we'll share our SOC2/ISO pack. for pilot we can provide a redacted pen-test summary and our security contact for a deeper review.
05:20 Priya Nair: latency vs cost — you mentioned batching and quantization suggestions in the docs. we care about p95 latency but also cost per inference.
05:28 Maya Chen: right — Redwood Optimize will suggest batching windows based on traffic pattern, and quantization profiles if your model supports it. for low-latency we recommend smaller batches with pre-warmed instances; for cost-sensitive workloads larger batch windows and KV cache. the console also simulates expected cost per 1M requests with current config.
05:54 Alex Ramos: are there any known limitations for structured outputs? edge cases?
06:00 Maya Chen: schema complexity can be a factor — deeply nested optional unions are harder to enforce. also, some open models have inconsistent tokenization that can break strict validation; that's where our strict-mode runtime and sanitizer tools come in. we also support synthetic evals to surface regressions.
06:24 Priya Nair: ok, show the console where we can author the schema and see runtime traces.
06:30 Maya Chen: (screen) here in the console we have schema editor with examples, a test harness to run against a prompt set, and a viz of calls showing fallback reasons and tool invocations. you can click into a single request and see: prompt, model, response, validator result, and any orchestrated tool calls.
07:02 Jordan Lee: quick note on integrations — we support webhooks, AWS lambda, GCP functions, and direct connectors for ServiceNow/JIRA if you want tickets to flow into your ITSM.
07:17 Alex Ramos: our flow uses an internal ticketing API, not ServiceNow. can we map action -> our endpoint with authentication?
07:24 Maya Chen: yes — the runtime supports signing requests with customer-managed keys and a per-endpoint credential. you can also restrict which tool actions are allowed per project via RBAC.
07:38 Jamal Ortiz: for the VPC pilot, our networking team wants to know about egress, IP ranges, and peering.
07:44 Jordan Lee: we'll provide a network diagram and CIDR ranges. in Private deployment we can peer directly; in hosted we provide a set of egress IPs and recommend IP allowlisting.
07:58 Priya Nair: curious about observability retention — can we export traces to datadog and raw logs to gcs?
08:04 Samir Patel: yes — we have integrations for Datadog/Prometheus and can stream raw logs to S3/GCS and events to your SIEM via syslog.
08:18 Hannah Lee: little nit — how do you do anomaly detection on quality regressions?
08:23 Maya Chen: Optimize has quality monitors — you supply a prompt set and expected outputs; we compute similarity metrics and regression alerts, tie them to a prompt-based eval so you get notified on quality drop after a model change.
08:40 Alex Ramos: can we run a perf benchmark against our payload shapes?
08:45 Maya Chen: absolutely, we can run a benchmark in your environment or ours. for pilot we usually run a synthetic throughput test with your schema and trace replay. results included: p50/p95/p99, token cost estimate, and KV cache hit rates.
09:00 Jordan Lee: ok let's sketch a pilot: 6 weeks, VPC peered deployment, sample of 10k requests/day, strict schema enforcement for ticketing and ETA. success criteria: p95 < 350ms, schema pass rate > 99%, and integration with your ticket endpoint.
09:22 Priya Nair: timeline?
09:25 Jordan Lee: if we get SOW signed within the week we can spin up the pilot in 2 weeks. 
09:31 Alex Ramos: fair. any competitive differences we should be mindful of? we tested GigaServe AI before and they had flaky tool mapping and opaque tracing.
09:40 Samir Patel: we've heard that — our emphasis is explicit typed-interfaces and per-request tracing. we also provide a console-first experience for debugging and policy-based fallback.
09:56 Maya Chen: little demo follow-up — i'll export a sample schema and runtime trace for the exact ticket flow you described and drop it in the shared drive.
10:05 Priya Nair: can you include pricing options for hosted and for a dedicated pool?
10:10 Jordan Lee: yes we'll include hosted per-token estimates, dedicated baseline, and Private deployment uplift in a pricing sheet.
10:18 Hannah Lee: for security, include steps for SOC2 review and an outline for the pen-test timeline.
10:24 Jordan Lee: noted. we'll share the compliance pack and a redacted pen-test summary.
10:35 Jamal Ortiz: last question — what happens if the runtime faces overload? do you offer graceful degradation?
10:40 Maya Chen: yes — smart routing will divert to a cost-tier or degrade to a smaller model, and there are automatic fallback policies to avoid full outage. you can configure automatic model downgrade, rate-limits, or circuit-breakers to protect downstream services.
10:58 Jordan Lee: okay, recap of next steps: we'll send SOW + pricing, SOC2/ISO docs, example schema + trace, and schedule pilot kickoff. any other asks?
11:12 Alex Ramos: please add our network CIDRs, and Priya will confirm the pilot contacts.
11:20 Jordan Lee: great thanks all. we'll follow up by email, end call.
